title: A Practitioner's Guide to Materials Theory and Computation in the Age of Big Data and Artificial Intelligence
authors: Jack Yang
abstract: Computational modelling has become a cornerstone of materials science, with advances in atomistic simulations, high-throughput computation, and artificial intelligence transforming how materials are understood, discovered, and designed. These developments build upon generations of theoretical innovations that have translated complex mathematical and physical principles into practical predictive tools. However, the growing diversity of computational methods presents challenges for practitioners seeking a coherent understanding of their theoretical foundations. Drawing upon the author's research experience, this monograph provides a practitioner-oriented, pedagogical overview of computational materials science, unified through the concepts of potential-energy landscapes and statistical sampling. It explores how these concepts underpin structural stability, phase behaviour, and electronic and magnetic properties, through a systematic treatment of empirical force fields, density-functional theory, many-body electronic-structure methods, statistical sampling, and property prediction. It further examines high-throughput workflows, materials databases, and the probabilistic foundations of artificial intelligence. Particular emphasis is placed on atomistic representations, graph neural networks, and generative models, highlighting the roles of symmetry, group theory, differential geometry, and stochastic processes in modern materials modelling. By connecting established physical theories with emerging data-driven approaches, this monograph offers a unified perspective on computational materials science and identifies opportunities and challenges toward physics-informed, efficient, and reliable materials discovery.

infographic.key_insight: Potential-energy landscapes and statistical sampling provide a unified framework connecting established materials theories with modern AI-driven discovery.
infographic.engineering_relevance: This framework can help practitioners choose and integrate simulation methods, high-throughput workflows, and AI tools for materials design.
method: Connect force fields, density-functional theory, and many-body methods through energy landscapes and sampling.
Review high-throughput workflows, materials databases, and probabilistic AI foundations.
Explain atomistic representations, graph neural networks, and generative models using symmetry and related mathematics.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract describes a pedagogical monograph informed by the author's research experience, without reporting datasets, benchmarks, or quantitative validation.
infographic.watch_item: The overview does not establish application-specific accuracy or reliability; selected methods still require validation for the target material and property.
infographic.paper_title: A Practitioner's Guide to Materials Theory and Computation in the Age of Big Data and Artificial Intelligence

title: IANN: A Unified Framework for Equivariant InterAtomic Neural Networks with User-Friendly Implementation
authors: Changzhi Ai, Xueping Qin, Dimosthenis Sokaras, Frank Abild-Pedersen, Johannes Voss
abstract: Machine-learning interatomic potentials (MLIPs) now approach density functional theory (DFT) accuracy at a fraction of its cost, but the practical benefit is limited by software fragmentation: each state-of-the-art architecture is released as a separate codebase, with its own data format, configuration system, training loop and molecular-dynamics interface. Comparing two architectures on the same dataset, or moving a trained model into a production simulation, therefore requires substantial re-engineering. We introduce IANN (InterAtomic Neural Network), an open-source PyTorch framework that reimplements equivariant graph neural networks - PaiNN, NequIP, MACE, Allegro, EquiformerV2, EquiformerV3 and UMA - behind a unified data object, a unified trainer and a single deployment route, so that the architecture is a one-word change in a configuration dictionary. Forces, stresses and virials are obtained for every architecture from one analytic differentiation of the energy with respect to the edge vectors of the atomic graph, exact under periodic boundary conditions. Distributed training is configured automatically from the SLURM, PBS or MPI environment, so the same script runs unchanged from a workstation to a multi-node GPU allocation. Self-describing checkpoints serve directly as ASE calculators, as ensembles reporting uncertainties, or as TorchScript models run inside LAMMPS through bundled C++ pair styles with single- and multi-GPU inference. Trained on a common dataset of millions of structures, the architectures can be compared under identical conditions. We further release PaiNN foundation models trained on 41.9 million curated DFT structures from MPtrj, Alexandria, OMat24, MatPES, OC20, OC22, OC25, MPr2SCAN and MatPESr2SCAN, spanning the PBE, RPBE and r2SCAN functionals. Additionally, IANN provides an agent interface to facilitate integration with autonomous agents.

infographic.key_insight: IANN unifies seven equivariant interatomic neural network architectures in one PyTorch framework, making architecture selection a one-word configuration change.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Shared training and deployment interfaces reduce re-engineering when comparing potentials or moving models into ASE and LAMMPS simulations.
method: Standardize atomic data, training and deployment across PaiNN, NequIP, MACE, Allegro, EquiformerV2, EquiformerV3 and UMA.
Derive forces, stresses and virials analytically from energy via atomic-graph edge vectors, including periodic boundaries.
Automatically configure distributed training and support self-describing checkpoints, uncertainty ensembles and TorchScript deployment.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports architecture comparisons on a shared dataset of millions of structures and releases PaiNN foundation models trained on 41.9 million curated DFT structures spanning PBE, RPBE and r2SCAN.
infographic.watch_item: The abstract provides no quantitative accuracy or speed benchmarks, so task-specific validation remains necessary before production use.
infographic.paper_title: IANN: A Unified Framework for Equivariant InterAtomic Neural Networks with User-Friendly Implementation

title: Adsorbate-Free Screening of Dissociative Water Adsorption on Nickel Nanoparticles via Graph Neural Networks
authors: Marta Monti, Alec Noppe, Olivier Lugier, Maria B. Brands, Bernd Ensing
abstract: Dissociative water adsorption is a key step in heterogeneous and electrochemical catalysis, but on finite Ni nanosystems the OH$^*$ and H$^*$ fragments can occupy many combinations of surface sites, making exhaustive density functional theory (DFT) screening impractical. We introduce a graph neural network (GNN) framework with an adsorbate-free representation: candidate O- and H-binding sites are defined by sets of Ni atoms (\textit{anchors}), and each site pair is encoded as a graph constructed solely from these anchors and their local Ni environment. Using only MACE-relaxed bare Ni geometries as input, separate GNNs predict the DFT-reference adsorption energies of OH$^*$+H$^*$ configurations and whether the proposed binding sites would be retained upon DFT relaxation, eliminating the need to construct or relax adsorbates during screening. Trained across Ni nanoclusters and Ni(111)/Ni(100) surfaces, the energy model achieves a mean absolute error of 0.031 eV on the internal validation set and demonstrates transferability to unseen Ni$_{55}$, Ni$_{91}$, and Ni$_{130}$ clusters and larger surface cells, particularly for relative-energy ranking, although quantitative accuracy varies across systems. These independent tests also support the retention classifier's use as a conservative filter for selecting configurations likely to preserve their proposed binding sites. Application to Ni nanoparticles containing up to $\sim$3000 atoms identifies favorable co-adsorption motifs and shows that lower O-site coordination generally stabilizes the dissociated state, whereas H-site coordination has a weaker influence. The framework thus offers an efficient route to screening adsorption energetics, with potential extensions to other metals and adsorbate combinations.

infographic.key_insight: Graph neural networks can screen dissociative water adsorption on nickel using only bare-metal geometries, without constructing or relaxing adsorbates during screening.
infographic.engineering_relevance: This approach reduces the cost of identifying favorable OH*+H* configurations on nickel nanoparticles relevant to heterogeneous and electrochemical catalysis.
method: Define candidate O- and H-binding sites using sets of nickel anchor atoms.
Build adsorbate-free graphs from anchors and their local environments in MACE-relaxed bare nickel structures.
Use separate GNNs to predict adsorption energies and whether proposed binding sites survive DFT relaxation.
infographic.evidence_signal: The energy model achieved 0.031 eV internal-validation MAE; independent tests covered unseen Ni55, Ni91, Ni130 clusters and larger surface cells, with particularly promising relative-energy ranking.
infographic.watch_item: Quantitative accuracy varies across systems, so deployment should validate energy predictions and retention filtering on representative target structures.
infographic.paper_title: Adsorbate-Free Screening of Dissociative Water Adsorption on Nickel Nanoparticles via Graph Neural Networks

title: Nahual: A Sequence Model for Language and Atoms
authors: Austin H. Cheng, Marcel Müller, Andreas Burger, Yeonghun Kang, Tsz Wai Ko, Marta Skreta
abstract: Generative models play a rapidly growing role in the design and simulation of molecules. The most widely used applications of generative models are in large language models (LLMs), owing to the natural flexibility of language for specifying and answering queries. However, generalist LLMs do not effectively handle large sets of 3D coordinates, whereas specialist generative models of 3D molecules cannot reach the controllability afforded by language. To bridge these capabilities, we propose Nahual, a decoder-only autoregressive diffusion model for any sequence of text and 3D molecules. To enable expressive autoregression on continuous coordinates, we propose next-token diffusion, whereby a causal transformer denoises each token while attending to the clean tokens before it, without increasing context size. We train Nahual on a curated set of twelve 3D chemistry tasks ranging from microsolvation to molecular conformer search to adsorption on metal surfaces, with associated evaluation metrics and baselines. The result is a single set of end-to-end-trained weights that simultaneously performs all tasks and surpasses state-of-the-art models specialized for crystal structure prediction and property-conditional molecule generation. Our results demonstrate the viability of scaling generalist decoder-only models for native multimodal understanding and generation across language and chemistry. Code is available at https://github.com/the-matter-lab/nahual.

infographic.key_insight: Nahual unifies language and 3D molecular generation in one decoder-only model, combining text-based control with native coordinate generation.
infographic.engineering_relevance: A single model could support workflows spanning molecular conformer search, microsolvation, crystal structure prediction, and adsorption on metal surfaces.
method: Uses a decoder-only autoregressive diffusion architecture for sequences of text and 3D molecules.
Applies next-token diffusion: a causal transformer denoises each token while attending to preceding clean tokens without increasing context size.
Trains one shared set of weights end to end across twelve 3D chemistry tasks.
infographic.evidence_signal: On a curated twelve-task dataset with associated metrics and baselines, the authors report surpassing specialized state-of-the-art models for crystal structure prediction and property-conditional molecule generation.
infographic.watch_item: The abstract does not quantify performance gains, inference cost, or generalization beyond the curated tasks, leaving deployment suitability uncertain.
infographic.paper_title: Nahual: A Sequence Model for Language and Atoms

title: A Density Functional Tight Binding Model for Rapid Screening of Spin-Orbit-Coupling-Driven Topological Properties in Bismuth
authors: Nir Goldman, Ben Hourahine
abstract: We present a transferable Density Functional Tight Binding (DFTB) model for bismuth with explicit spin-orbit coupling that enables exploration of the structural degrees of freedom governing topological properties with minimal computational resources. We have used our DFTB model to run high-throughput calculations at a scale that would be significantly more expensive with standard Kohn-Sham Density Functional Theory (DFT) to determine a strain-buckling map of electronic and topological properties for bismuthene, where we identify regions of band gap closure and band inversion as a function of structural parameters. We show that our approach yields an accurate band structure for the rhombohedral phase, where small band gaps exist at or near time-reversal-invariant momentum (TRIM) points. We then demonstrate the transferability of our model to bismuth properties not included in our training data through determination of the rhombohedral phase phonon density of states and energetic ordering of additional bismuth solid phases. Finally, we have validated our topological predictions through comparison to DFT results for the optimized bilayer geometries, a band inversion order parameter, and the $\mathbb{Z}_2$ invariant as a function of monolayer unit cell length. Our efforts establish DFTB as a rigorous approach for topological characterization while yielding approximately three orders of magnitude increase in computational efficiency relative to DFT. Our model can thus serve as a computational tool for topological materials discovery by enabling large-scale computational screening to address the potentially complex relationship between physical-chemical properties and the resulting topological classification.

infographic.key_insight: A bismuth density functional tight binding (DFTB) model with explicit spin–orbit coupling enables topological screening at approximately 1,000 times the computational efficiency of standard DFT.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The model makes large-scale screening of strain and buckling practical for identifying bismuthene structures with promising electronic and topological properties.
method: Develop a transferable bismuth DFTB model with explicit spin–orbit coupling.
Map band-gap closure and band inversion across bismuthene strain and buckling.
Validate topology against DFT using optimized bilayers, a band-inversion order parameter, and the Z₂ invariant.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports accurate rhombohedral band structures, transferability tests on phonon density of states and solid-phase energy ordering, and topological validation against DFT.
infographic.watch_item: Validation is specific to the studied bismuth structures; reliability beyond the tested structural range or in other materials requires further assessment.
infographic.paper_title: A Density Functional Tight Binding Model for Rapid Screening of Spin-Orbit-Coupling-Driven Topological Properties in Bismuth

title: Energetics of Coherent Heterophase Interfaces: Separating Chemical and Strain Contributions
authors: Adolfo Salgado-Casanova, Jacob Pietryga, Yi Xia, Chris Wolverton
abstract: Coherent interfacial energies govern the formation and evolution of multiphase microstructures, but their calculation is complicated by the elastic energy required to accommodate lattice mismatch. Here, we construct a high-throughput DFT database of 365 coherent FCC/FCC, BCC/BCC, and HCP/HCP interfaces involving 41 metallic elements and lattice mismatches of up to 25%. We use the supercell approach, consisting of constructing superlattices of different thicknesses to separate the coherency strain energy from the chemical contribution to the interfacial energy. We classify the results according to the long-range ordering tendency of each binary system and the sign of the calculated interfacial energy. Most phase-separating systems exhibit positive interfacial energies, whereas most compound-ordering systems exhibit negative values, reflecting favorable unlike-atom bonding. Exceptions show that the chemical preference at a particular interface need not coincide with bulk phase behavior: coherency strain can oppose ordering, and stable compounds can adopt structures distinct from the calculated superlattices. No clear correlation of interfacial energy with lattice mismatch is observed, whereas coherency strain energy increases with mismatch. For phase-separating systems, the lowest interfacial energies generally occur along the closest-packed orientations, while this trend is absent for ordering systems. Comparisons with reported interfacial energies and binary phase diagrams show qualitative consistency, although quantitative agreement varies with reference states, structural constraints, and temperature. The database provides a systematic reference for metallic coherent heterophase interfaces and demonstrates the importance of separating strain and chemical energy contributions when interpreting alloy behavior.

infographic.key_insight: Separating chemical and coherency strain contributions reveals that coherent interface energies reflect bonding preferences rather than lattice mismatch alone.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The database offers a reference for interpreting metallic alloy microstructures without conflating interfacial chemistry with elastic strain costs.
method: Compute 365 coherent FCC/FCC, BCC/BCC, and HCP/HCP interfaces using high-throughput DFT.
Vary superlattice thickness to separate coherency strain energy from chemical interfacial energy.
Classify results by bulk ordering tendency, interface-energy sign, and crystallographic orientation.
infographic.evidence_signal: Across 41 metallic elements and lattice mismatches up to 25%, most phase-separating systems have positive interface energies and most ordering systems have negative values; strain energy, but not interface energy, increases with mismatch.
infographic.watch_item: Quantitative comparisons depend on reference states, imposed coherent structures, and temperature; interface bonding preferences need not match bulk phase behavior.
infographic.paper_title: Energetics of Coherent Heterophase Interfaces: Separating Chemical and Strain Contributions

title: Large-scale Monte Carlo/Molecular Dynamics simulations with Atomic Cluster Expansion potentials in LAMMPS
authors: Lorenzo Piersante, Anirudh Raju Natarajan
abstract: Monte Carlo/molecular dynamics (MCMD) simulations are widely used to study the properties of materials at the mesoscale. Simulations with hundreds of thousands of atoms usually rely on empirical potentials because MCMD with machine-learning interatomic potentials is impractical at this scale in existing implementations. Here, we introduce a hybrid MPI/OpenMP scheme for MCMD with Atomic Cluster Expansion (ACE) potentials in LAMMPS. Monte Carlo moves are evaluated from local energy changes and carried out in parallel over MPI ranks, while molecular dynamics is parallelized over OpenMP threads. At a fixed number of CPUs, the wall time of the Monte Carlo moves decreases by a factor equal to the number of MPI ranks. Larger simulation cells also reduce the statistical errors of free energy calculations because thermal fluctuations decrease with system size. We demonstrate the scheme by calculating free energies of the HCP and BCC phases in the strongly anharmonic Hf--Ti system and by simulating zirconium segregation in a nanocrystalline copper sample of 670,000 atoms. For Cu--Zr, an ACE potential and an empirical potential predict similar grain boundary compositions but different amounts of zirconium dissolved in the grains. The scheme makes MCMD simulations with machine-learning interatomic potentials practical at the length scales of microstructure.

infographic.key_insight: A hybrid MPI/OpenMP implementation in LAMMPS makes Monte Carlo/molecular dynamics with Atomic Cluster Expansion potentials practical for microstructure-scale simulations.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The scheme enables machine-learning-potential studies of phase stability and grain-boundary segregation in systems containing hundreds of thousands of atoms.
method: Evaluate Monte Carlo moves using local energy changes.
Distribute Monte Carlo moves across MPI ranks and parallelize molecular dynamics over OpenMP threads.
Use larger simulation cells to reduce thermal fluctuations and statistical errors in free-energy calculations.
infographic.evidence_signal: Demonstrations include HCP/BCC free energies in Hf–Ti and zirconium segregation in 670,000-atom nanocrystalline copper; at fixed CPU count, Monte Carlo wall time decreases by a factor equal to the number of MPI ranks.
infographic.watch_item: Predicted segregation remains potential-dependent: ACE and empirical potentials give similar grain-boundary compositions but different zirconium solubilities within grains.
infographic.paper_title: Large-scale Monte Carlo/Molecular Dynamics simulations with Atomic Cluster Expansion potentials in LAMMPS

title: Validating Graph Neural Network Feature Attribution Through Local Perturbations: A Study on CoMoFeNiCu Decomposition Enthalpy
authors: Miguel Tenorio, James Chapman
abstract: Graph neural networks (GNNs) show promise for predicting materials properties, but interpretability remains a challenge, particularly understanding whether attributed feature importance reflects physical reality or statistical artifacts. Here, we present a methods validation study that deliberately overfits a physics-aware GNN ensemble to probe the robustness of feature-ranking approaches. Using the CoMoFeNiCu high-entropy alloy system with three stoichiometries, we train GNNs to predict decomposition enthalpies from DFT-calculated structures while explicitly constraining output weights to encode feature importance. By design, our dataset is limited (approximately 900 binary and 4,500 ternary decomposition pathways) to control compositional complexity and enable precise interrogation of local chemistry effects. We validate that feature rankings capture meaningful local-environment information through a series of atomic swap perturbations: perturbing individual atomic sites and re-ranking features reveals spatial decay consistent with the GNN's interaction cutoff, confirming that weights encode neighbor-shell effects rather than global stoichiometric artifacts alone. Results demonstrate that feature attribution methods can remain physically interpretable even under overfitting, provided validation is rigorous. This work establishes a foundation for trustworthy interpretability in materials GNNs and sets the stage for scaling to multiple chemistries and testing generalization across compositional spaces.

infographic.key_insight: Local atomic-swap tests indicate that GNN feature rankings can capture physically meaningful neighbor-shell effects even under deliberate overfitting.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Perturbation-based validation can help engineers assess whether materials-model explanations reflect local chemistry rather than only compositional correlations.
method: Train a deliberately overfit, physics-aware GNN ensemble on DFT-derived CoMoFeNiCu decomposition enthalpies.
Constrain output weights to encode feature importance.
Swap atoms at individual sites and re-rank features to test spatial sensitivity.
infographic.evidence_signal: Across three stoichiometries with approximately 900 binary and 4,500 ternary decomposition pathways, attribution changes showed spatial decay consistent with the GNN interaction cutoff.
infographic.watch_item: Validation is limited to a deliberately overfit model in one alloy system; generalization across chemistries and compositions remains untested.
infographic.paper_title: Validating Graph Neural Network Feature Attribution Through Local Perturbations: A Study on CoMoFeNiCu Decomposition Enthalpy

title: Materials research with a general-purpose agent
authors: Paulo R. Pires, Théo Cavignac, Tiago F. T. Cerqueira, Hai-Chen Wang, Silvana Botti, Miguel A. L. Marques
abstract: Over the last decade we have built Alexandria, an open database of about 15 million density-functional calculations of crystals. It includes PBE, PBEsol, SCAN and TB-mBJ results, structures relaxed at pressures up to 150 GPa, dielectric tensors and about 145,000 electron-phonon calculations, together with more than 400 million structures relaxed with machine-learned potentials. On these data we trained a generative model for crystal structures, a universal interatomic potential and graph neural networks for more than ten properties, from band gaps to superconducting critical temperatures. From the convex hull we computed a reaction graph of the 17.4 billion reactions between its 193,416 stable compounds. Here we give all of this to a general-purpose language-model agent. Working unattended, the agent screens the database for a solar absorber, drops a candidate whose synthesis releases too little energy, and writes a synthesis plan with precursors, crucible and atmosphere. Asked about the well-studied Ba-Zr-S system, it finds an unreported sulfide and designs the experiment that would confirm or rule it out. Asked for an air-stable alternative, it designs one and tests it against new structures from the generative model. With web search alone, the same agent proposes what the literature already discusses. Put together, the data, the models and the reaction graph let a general agent do what none of them does alone: go from a question in plain words to an experiment that a laboratory can run and test.

infographic.key_insight: A general-purpose language-model agent combines materials databases, predictive models and reaction graphs to turn plain-language questions into testable synthesis plans.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The workflow connects candidate screening to practical experimental choices, including precursors, crucibles and atmospheres.
method: Equip the agent with Alexandria data, crystal-generation models and property predictors.
Use reaction energetics to screen candidates and assess synthesis routes.
Design experiments and challenge proposed materials against newly generated structures.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports about 15 million density-functional calculations and a graph of 17.4 billion reactions, with unattended case studies producing proposals beyond a web-search-only baseline.
infographic.watch_item: The abstract describes computational proposals, not laboratory-confirmed synthesis or performance.
infographic.paper_title: Materials research with a general-purpose agent

title: A database of optical and thermal-radiative behaviour of materials under solar radiation
authors: Vasiliki E. Alexopoulou, Nikolaos Karalis, Konstantinos Asimakopoulos, Andrei Totu, Constantin Sandu, Paul-Peter Sotiriadis
abstract: Solar-matter interactions are important in many scientific and engineering applications. Modeling them needs consistent optical and thermal-radiative properties over the full solar spectrum. Here we present SpaderOptics, a database for 21 materials: metals, oxides, semiconductors, polymers, ceramics, and carbon. It compiles wavelength-dependent refractive indices and extinction coefficients from the literature. Each literature source is kept separate, together with its original conditions. One physics-based calculation chain turns these data into reflectivity, transmissivity, absorptivity, and emissivity for different incidence angles, slab thicknesses, and temperatures. Combined with the Air Mass Zero (AM0) solar spectrum, the properties give absorbed, reflected, and transmitted solar flux for concentrated sunlight. Equilibrium temperatures are given for both a theoretical lumped body and for a slab body, in which thermal conduction is considered. All data are limited to the solid state, up to a material-specific upper temperature limit. Currently, the database applies to extraterrestrial (AM0) sunlight only. A graphical App is also provided for exploring and visualizing the database.

infographic.key_insight: SpaderOptics links wavelength-dependent optical data for 21 materials to solar-energy absorption and thermal-radiative behaviour.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The database supports material selection and thermal modeling under concentrated extraterrestrial sunlight.
method: Compile literature refractive indices and extinction coefficients, preserving each source and its original conditions.
Calculate reflectivity, transmissivity, absorptivity, and emissivity across incidence angles, slab thicknesses, and temperatures.
Combine these properties with AM0 sunlight to calculate solar fluxes and equilibrium temperatures for lumped and thermally conducting slab bodies.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports coverage of 21 materials across six classes, but provides no quantitative validation results.
infographic.watch_item: Current use is limited to extraterrestrial AM0 sunlight and solid-state temperatures below material-specific upper limits.
infographic.paper_title: A database of optical and thermal-radiative behaviour of materials under solar radiation

title: Determining Concentration from Raman Spectroscopy with Manifold Learning and Y-shaped Conformal Autoencoders
authors: Anna Taka, Eleni D. Koronaki, Ioannis G. Kevrekidis, Eike Cramer, Joern Viell, Alexander Mitsos
abstract: Monitoring of chemical processes is crucial in chemical engineering, motivating sophisticated process analytical technology (PAT). In-line analytics are advantageous, with Raman spectroscopy being an established and reliable tool in various applications, from which many properties can be determined. We recently [Koronaki et al., AIChEJ 2024] proposed determining polymer particle size from Raman spectroscopic data, by combining Diffusion Maps (a manifold learning method) with a Y-shaped Conformal Autoencoder Neural Network. Herein, we extend this workflow to predict liquid concentrations, allowing also for multiple target predictions from the same model. We apply the methods on two datasets consisting of Raman measurements and concentration measurements: one from microgel polymerization and one from citric acid dissociation. The single-target concentration prediction results, where one target is determined from each model at a time, are accurate. Comparing against dedicated methods such as Indirect Hard Modeling (IHM) is not straightforward, due to the different validation strategies and the considered spectra range; nevertheless, it is fair to say that IHM performs slightly better than the proposed workflow. We further compare this approach with other regression methods, such as artificial neural networks, extreme gradient boosting and partial least squares, and the results show that the Conformal Autoencoders achieve higher predictive performance, demonstrating that the workflow can also be used for concentration determination. Finally we find that single-target concentration predictions are more accurate than the multiple target predictions for both case studies.

infographic.key_insight: Diffusion Maps combined with Y-shaped Conformal Autoencoders predict liquid concentrations from Raman spectra, with single-target models outperforming multi-target models.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The workflow supports Raman-based in-line concentration monitoring for chemical process analytics.
method: Apply Diffusion Maps for manifold learning on Raman spectra.
Use Y-shaped Conformal Autoencoders to predict one or multiple concentration targets.
Compare predictions with neural networks, extreme gradient boosting, and partial least squares.
infographic.evidence_signal: Across microgel polymerization and citric acid dissociation datasets, the authors report accurate single-target predictions and higher predictive performance than the tested regression alternatives.
infographic.watch_item: Indirect Hard Modeling performed slightly better, but differing validation strategies and spectral ranges limit direct comparison.
infographic.paper_title: Determining Concentration from Raman Spectroscopy with Manifold Learning and Y-shaped Conformal Autoencoders

title: Scaling laws in machine learning on non-ideal experimental data enable inverse design of radiative-cooling coatings
authors: Kunihiko Shizume, Jiawen Li, Yaerim Lee, Yuki Asano, Tuwei Liao, Koji Tsuda
abstract: Materials informatics increasingly targets multicomponent materials, yet experimental datasets inevitably contain non-ideal variations arising from imperfect uniformity and reproducibility in composition, coating formation, and measurement. Whether machine-learning prediction accuracy scales with amount of data under these conditions remains unclear. Here, we develop an automated platform that produced and optically characterized 11,520 radiative-cooling coatings spanning nine material and processing parameters. Forward and inverse neural networks, and a spectrum-conditioned diffusion model were trained on subsets of 10 to 10,000 samples. All models exhibited power-law scaling, with prediction errors decreasing with dataset size. Experimental inverse-design validation showed that larger datasets produced spectra closer to a broadband-emitter target. The diffusion model generated multiple candidate parameter sets, allowing selection among alternative solutions based on ease of fabrication, cost, and scalability. These results demonstrate predictable learning-curve scaling in non-ideal experimental data and provide a quantitative basis for estimating the benefit of additional experimental data, and thus the cost-effectiveness of materials-informatics.

infographic.key_insight: Prediction errors followed power-law decreases as training datasets grew, despite non-ideal experimental variability in radiative-cooling coatings.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Learning curves can help estimate the value of additional experiments, while inverse models propose coating designs that can be screened for fabrication ease, cost, and scalability.
method: Automate fabrication and optical characterization across nine material and processing parameters.
Train forward and inverse neural networks and a spectrum-conditioned diffusion model on 10–10,000 samples.
Experimentally validate inverse designs against a broadband-emitter target.
infographic.evidence_signal: The platform produced 11,520 coatings; all model types exhibited power-law error scaling, and larger training datasets yielded experimentally validated spectra closer to the target.
infographic.watch_item: Scaling demonstrated for this coating platform may not transfer to other material systems or fabrication conditions without validation.
infographic.paper_title: Scaling laws in machine learning on non-ideal experimental data enable inverse design of radiative-cooling coatings

title: Metallic or insulating magnetic phases of transition-metal oxides in light of the Slater vs Mott controversy
authors: Xiuwen Zhang, Jia-Xin Xiong, Alex Zunger
abstract: Magnetic d-electron oxides usually have a long-range-ordered ground state and an above-ground-state disordered para phase. The historical Slater-Mott controversy still reverberating to date pertains to understanding the origin of the insulating vs metallic nature of these two phases. Slater suggested that the insulating character evolved from the long-range order (LRO) antiferromagnetic (AFM) cell-doubling, leading to energy band repulsion and thus to forming a band gap. The reliance on LRO to explain gapping suggests that the absence of LRO in the spin-disordered para-phase would deprive the system from band repulsion, thus predicting a metallic paramagnetic (PM) phase. This, however, conflicts with numerous current observations. The alternative Mott-Peierls-Hubbard view abandons the mean-field-like band structure view emphasizing instead the local interelectronic repulsion U as a strong correlation signature of gapping both at the presence or absence of LRO. However, U is not an easily measured or calculated quantity in periodic systems, a situation often leading in practice to treating U as an adjustable parameter. The current work uses a parameter-free mean-field-like approach (Density Functional Theory, DFT), allowing energy-lowering symmetry breaking. This is done by considering local magnetic motifs as building blocks of the macroscopic AFM or PM phases. It is found that even when such motifs are isolated electronically from each other (i.e. vanishing LRO) by embedding them in quantum barriers (such as magnetic NiO6 octahedra surrounded locally by wide-gap MgO) they exhibit an intrinsic band gap. Thus, the origin of the band gaps in AFM or PM phases need not be LRO or strong correlation and can be understood within the mean-field-like band structure approach with symmetry breaking.

infographic.key_insight: Magnetic transition-metal oxides can exhibit intrinsic band gaps without long-range magnetic order or an explicit strong-correlation mechanism when local symmetry breaking is allowed.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Local magnetic motifs offer a route to modeling insulating oxide phases without relying on an adjustable Hubbard U parameter.
method: Use parameter-free, mean-field-like density functional theory with energy-lowering symmetry breaking.
Represent antiferromagnetic and paramagnetic phases through local magnetic motifs.
Electronically isolate magnetic motifs using wide-gap barriers, including NiO6 octahedra embedded in MgO.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports that electronically isolated magnetic motifs retain intrinsic band gaps even as long-range magnetic order vanishes, but provides no numerical gap values or error metrics.
infographic.watch_item: The abstract does not establish quantitative accuracy across oxide chemistries or realistic finite-temperature paramagnetic states.
infographic.paper_title: Metallic or insulating magnetic phases of transition-metal oxides in light of the Slater vs Mott controversy

title: Crystal Structure Prediction from Search to Learning: A 30-Year Expedition
authors: Jianjun Hu, Ying Feng
abstract: Crystal structure prediction (CSP) determines periodic atomic or molecular arrangements from chemical composition and physical conditions. Over three decades, CSP has evolved from chemical construction and global energy optimization to hybrid approaches combining symmetry, learned potentials, adaptive search, and deep generative models. This survey reviews method, software, review, and benchmark records from 1996 to October 2026, covering inorganic and molecular crystals, including formula-conditioned diffusion, flow, and autoregressive models that preserve composition. We classify methods by candidate construction and exploration: template and discrete construction, random search, evolutionary search, swarm and differential evolution, energy-landscape exploration, adaptive machine-learning-guided search, and learned generation. We distinguish representation, relaxation, ranking, and physical qualification. Benchmarks reveal no universally dominant approach. In a 46-target leaderboard snapshot, the best-performing template method achieves higher top-1 recovery than leading generative models, but paired tests show no statistically significant differences from several generative competitors. We also audit predictions for 68 experimentally examined materials, including 52 with structures confirmed by diffraction or microscopy. Predictions for 23 of the 68 preceded experiment, mostly through first-principles global search. Within the reviewed evidence, we find no independently confirmed discovery in which a deep generative model predicted the structure before experiment. We conclude with the principal limitations of current CSP algorithms and priorities for future research.

infographic.key_insight: Crystal structure prediction has evolved from global search to learned generation, but reviewed benchmarks show no universally dominant approach.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Reliable materials workflows should combine candidate generation with relaxation, ranking, and physical validation rather than rely on generation alone.
method: Survey CSP methods, software, reviews, and benchmarks from 1996 to October 2026.
Classify approaches from template construction and global search to ML-guided search and learned generation.
Separate representation, relaxation, ranking, and physical qualification.
infographic.evidence_signal: A 46-target benchmark showed the best template method leading top-1 recovery without statistically significant paired differences from several generative competitors; an experimental audit covered 68 materials, including 52 structurally confirmed cases.
infographic.watch_item: Within the reviewed evidence, no independently confirmed discovery used a deep generative model to predict the structure before experiment.
infographic.paper_title: Crystal Structure Prediction from Search to Learning: A 30-Year Expedition

title: How many events does entanglement-based positronium imaging need? Information limits of Compton polarimetry with CZT detectors
authors: Haitao Zhou, Ruonan Wang, Jianyong Hu, Zhifang Wu, Sijin Li
abstract: The degree of polarisation correlation of the two annihilation photons, measured by Compton polarimetry, has been proposed as a PET biomarker of tissue microstructure, but the statistics it requires have not been quantified. We parameterise the measurement by the linear-polarisation correlation coefficient $κ$ ($κ=1$ maximally entangled, $1/2$ separable), derive the classical Fisher information of double-Compton events and compare it with the quantum Fisher information, relate $κ$ to the annihilation channels of positronium in tissue, and simulate pixelated CdZnTe (CZT) rings. The model is checked against three published measurements and an independent GATE/Geant4 simulation. A double-Compton event carries at most 0.12-0.14 units of Fisher information about $κ$ and 0.015 on average, 0.1-0.6% of the quantum limit. Event-wise maximum likelihood reaches the Cramer-Rao bound, whereas the conventional ratio R needs 1.2-2.3 times more events. The observed coefficient is $κ_{obs}=1-α(1-κ_{pick})$, with a pick-off share $α$ of 0.13-0.29 in tissue; it is sensitive to lipid fraction but not to oxygen, and carries no tissue information if pick-off photons are maximally entangled. Published porous-polymer data imply $κ_{pick}$ = 0.34-0.58. In a 15-mm CZT module, ordering ambiguity, position errors and electron transport roughly halve the information per event, and sequence reconstruction of multi-site events recovers this loss. With $^{18}$F and an eight-module ring, $κ$ can be measured to $\pm0.01$ in a 10-mm tumour, but separating tissues by $κ$ alone requires 6-74 times more decays than are available.

infographic.key_insight: Entanglement-based positronium imaging is statistically demanding: double-Compton events retain only 0.1–0.6% of the quantum information limit for measuring polarisation correlation.
infographic.engineering_relevance: CZT detector design, multi-site sequence reconstruction and event-wise maximum likelihood can improve information recovery, but tissue discrimination remains limited by event counts.
method: Derive classical Fisher information for polarisation correlation κ and compare with the quantum limit.
Relate κ to positronium annihilation channels and tissue pick-off fractions.
Simulate pixelated CZT rings and compare event-wise maximum likelihood with the conventional ratio estimator.
infographic.evidence_signal: The model was checked against three published measurements and an independent GATE/Geant4 simulation; simulated double-Compton events carried 0.015 Fisher-information units on average.
infographic.watch_item: Under the studied ¹⁸F eight-module-ring conditions, distinguishing tissues by κ alone requires 6–74 times more decays than available, despite achievable ±0.01 precision in a 10-mm tumour.
infographic.paper_title: How many events does entanglement-based positronium imaging need? Information limits of Compton polarimetry with CZT detectors

title: Scaled boundary finite elements for FFT-based computational micromechanics
authors: Flavia Gehrig, Carolin Birk, Matti Schneider
abstract: We introduce a matrix-free FFT-based solver for three-dimensional linear elastic homogenization problems discretized by the scaled boundary finite element method (SBFEM) on a voxel grid. Owing to its analytical solution in the radial direction, the SBFEM discretization is inherently softer than fully integrated voxel finite elements, whereas its displacement-based formulation remains symmetric, conforming, and supports arbitrary stiffness anisotropy. These properties make SBFEM an attractive candidate for porous and highly heterogeneous microstructures, where existing voxel-based FFT discretizations offer no generally reliable choice: Reduced-integration hexahedral elements, equivalently the rotated staggered grid discretization, may suffer from hourglass instabilities in the presence of voids, whereas fully integrated hexahedral elements are often too stiff. The proposed discretization uses hexahedral SBFEM cells on the full voxel mesh of a regular periodic grid, retaining the simplicity of a fixed-resolution voxel representation without requiring adaptive mesh coarsening. The main contribution is a preconditioner based on the homogeneous SBFEM stiffness operator. We show that this preconditioner may be applied locally in Fourier space and that the condition number of the preconditioned system is bounded by the material contrast, independently of the grid resolution. This result enables a fully matrix-free implementation of the SBFEM-discretized problem, without assembling or storing the global stiffness matrix. Numerical experiments on a short-fibre reinforced composite, a polyurethane foam and a sand-based binder jet microstructure demonstrate robust convergence and competitive accuracy compared with established voxel discretizations. In particular, SBFEM remains stable for porous microstructures, for which reduced-integration hexahedral elements become unstable.

infographic.key_insight: Combining scaled boundary finite elements with an FFT-based solver enables stable, matrix-free elastic homogenization of porous and highly heterogeneous voxel microstructures.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The approach offers an alternative to overly stiff fully integrated voxel elements and potentially unstable reduced-integration elements for composites and porous materials.
method: Discretize a periodic voxel grid with hexahedral SBFEM cells using analytical radial solutions.
Apply a homogeneous SBFEM preconditioner locally in Fourier space without assembling the global stiffness matrix.
Bound the preconditioned condition number by material contrast, independently of grid resolution.
infographic.evidence_signal: Tests on a short-fibre composite, polyurethane foam and sand-based binder jet microstructure showed robust convergence and competitive accuracy, including stability in porous cases where reduced-integration elements became unstable.
infographic.watch_item: The demonstrated scope is three-dimensional linear elasticity on regular periodic voxel grids; nonlinear and nonperiodic applications are not established by the abstract.
infographic.paper_title: Scaled boundary finite elements for FFT-based computational micromechanics

title: Scaling a Universal Graph Neural Network Force Field to Billions of Atoms on Desk-Side GPUs
authors: Jaehyung Lee, Kamal Choudhary
abstract: Machine-learning force fields are capable of simulating billions of atoms, but usually require high-performance supercomputing clusters. We show that a universal graph neural network force field, ALIGNN-FF, evaluates energies and forces of more than one billion atoms on desk-side computers such as the NVIDIA GB10, which has 128 GB of unified memory, by using a cube-and-halo decomposition. The halo contains every atom within the model's 20 Å receptive field, which makes the result exact. One GB10 holds 216,000 atoms with forces as a single graph. The cube-and-halo decomposition removes this limit, enabling an evaluation of 2 billion atoms on nine GB10s. We also demonstrate three case studies: a billion-atom polycrystal, a 102-million-atom microelectronic gate stack and a 1.07-million-atom satellite tobacco mosaic virus in water. This brings single-point evaluations at experimentally relevant sizes within reach of one research group. The code is available at: https://github.com/atomgptlab/scalingmat.

infographic.key_insight: Cube-and-halo decomposition scales the universal ALIGNN-FF force field to billion-atom energy and force evaluations on desk-side GPUs.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The approach makes experimentally relevant structures accessible to individual research groups without requiring a supercomputing cluster.
method: Partition the atomic structure into cubes for separate evaluation.
Include halo atoms spanning the model’s full 20 Å receptive field to preserve exact results.
Distribute cube evaluations across memory-limited desk-side GPUs.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports 2-billion-atom evaluation on nine NVIDIA GB10s and demonstrations on a billion-atom polycrystal, a 102-million-atom gate stack, and a 1.07-million-atom virus-in-water system.
infographic.watch_item: The reported scale concerns single-point evaluations; it does not establish practical molecular-dynamics throughput or force-field accuracy across all demonstrated systems.
infographic.paper_title: Scaling a Universal Graph Neural Network Force Field to Billions of Atoms on Desk-Side GPUs

title: Mesoscale Neural Operators: Learning Nonlinear Constitutive Laws from Molecular Dynamics for Scalable Fracture Predictions
authors: Yue Yu, Jihong Wang, Stewart Silling, Ziwei Yang
abstract: Molecular dynamics (MD) simulations can capture the nanoscale physics of fracture at the atomistic level, but their computational cost prohibits predictions at the length scales and time scales needed for many applications. Machine learning approaches, on the other hand, have been proposed as heuristic surrogates for material fracture, yet they cannot guarantee the physical consistency of the predicted response. To address this shortcoming, we propose the mesoscale neural operator (MNO): a data-driven nonlocal constitutive model that is learned directly from MD loading and displacement data. After training, it can be used in continuum fracture simulations on much larger domains and grid sizes. The key idea of the MNO is to exploit the built-in characteristic length of a nonlocal model, called the horizon, to travel across scales. Physical consistency across scales is obtained by building two structural ingredients into the MNO: a normalized kernel that renders the strain energy density invariant under horizon rescaling, and a rescaled critical bond stretch that keeps the energy release rate consistent across scales. Through tests on synthetic data, we show that the MNO and its learning workflow indeed discover the nonlocal continuum multiscale model in the form of the nonlocal kernel and the nonlinear constitutive relation. We then apply the framework to coarse-grained MD data and find that in a test problem, the learned model matches the MD strain energy density and critical energy release rate within 3%. It also predicts the peak transmitted forces within 6% in out-of-distribution tension tests. As a further demonstration, the model is applied to a plate with 4000 times the area of the training specimens and containing an initial defect. In this problem, the model reproduces the main features of dynamic brittle fracture, including branch and cascading branch networks.

infographic.key_insight: Mesoscale neural operators learn nonlocal constitutive laws from molecular dynamics data while preserving key fracture energetics across scales.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The approach enables continuum fracture simulations on much larger domains and coarser grids than atomistic simulations can practically handle.
method: Learn a nonlocal kernel and nonlinear constitutive relation from MD loading and displacement data.
Normalize the kernel to preserve strain energy density under horizon rescaling.
Rescale critical bond stretch to maintain consistent energy release rates across scales.
infographic.evidence_signal: Synthetic tests supported model recovery; an MD-based test matched fracture energetics within 3%, out-of-distribution tension tests predicted peak forces within 6%, and a plate demonstration reproduced branching fracture over 4000× the training-specimen area.
infographic.watch_item: The reported tests do not establish transferability to other materials or loading regimes without additional validation.
infographic.paper_title: Mesoscale Neural Operators: Learning Nonlinear Constitutive Laws from Molecular Dynamics for Scalable Fracture Predictions

title: A Machine-learning-aided Workflow for Sampling Small Polaron Dynamics in Energy Materials
authors: Tavinder Singh, Harald Oberhofer
abstract: One of the defining characteristics of most energy materials, used as e.g.~battery electrodes, photovoltaics, or photocatalysts, is their ability conduct charges such as electrons and holes. The exact mechanism of this conductivity depends on the material, but is often dominated by the existence of mobile small polarons, i.e.~electrons or holes strongly localised through the polarisation of their environment. Computationally, small polarons can be treated with reasonably accuracy through the use of self-interaction corrected or hybrid density functional theory (DFT) together with local geometry optimisation. Similar approaches can be employed to determine the energy barriers to movement of the polarons through hopping. Unfortunately, realistic energy materials tend have very large numbers of symmetry inequivalent polaronic configurations and correspondingly large numbers of hopping barriers, making them hard to tackle explicitly. In this work we therefore extend the computational reach of DFT calculations with machine-learned (ML) surrogate models, which then feed into a kinetic model to quantitatively estimate the conductivity of a battery anode material (Li$_4$Ti$_5$O$_12$ or LTO) at realistic, defected conditions. We calculate the conductivity at room temperature to be 6.7 $\times$ 10$^{-3}$ S/cm which lies well in the experimental range. To this end, we only needed a total of 154 polaron barrier calculations, out of 3649 symmetry inequivalent ones, achieving an over 20-fold increase of computational efficiency. Overall, our work demonstrates how DFT-trained ML surrogates can be used to quantitatively and efficiently sample the dynamics of small polarons in energy materials.

infographic.key_insight: DFT-trained machine-learning surrogates enable efficient sampling of small-polaron hopping to predict charge conductivity in energy materials.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The workflow reduces the computational cost of predicting charge transport in defect-containing Li₄Ti₅O₁₂ battery anodes.
method: Calculate small-polaron hopping barriers using density functional theory.
Train ML surrogates to estimate barriers across polaron configurations.
Feed surrogate predictions into a kinetic model to estimate conductivity.
infographic.evidence_signal: Using 154 of 3,649 symmetry-inequivalent barrier calculations, the workflow achieved over 20-fold computational efficiency and predicted room-temperature conductivity of 6.7 × 10⁻³ S/cm, within the experimental range.
infographic.watch_item: Transferability to other materials or defect conditions requires validation beyond the demonstrated Li₄Ti₅O₁₂ case.
infographic.paper_title: A Machine-learning-aided Workflow for Sampling Small Polaron Dynamics in Energy Materials

title: Atomistic Insights into the All-Optical Switching of GdCo Alloys with Minimal Gd Concentration
authors: Paul-Iulian Gavriloaea, Jackson L. Ross, Richard F. L. Evans, Roy Chantrell, Stéphane Mangin, Oksana Chubykalo-Fesenko
abstract: Single-pulse all-optical helicity-independent switching (AO-HIS) is most commonly observed in Gd-based ferrimagnets near magnetization compensation. Recent experiments, however, demonstrated switching in Pt/Co/Pt-based heterostructures containing only a small amount of Gd at a Co/Pt interface. Here, we use atomistic spin-dynamics simulations to test an effective interfacial GdCo-alloy picture and to determine how species-dependent spin-bath coupling controls the minimum Gd concentration required for reversal. We compare a three-monolayer Co film with Gd confined to the surface layer and a three-dimensional uniformly alloyed GdCo model. Within the present uniform-heating model, robust transient toggle-like reversal is obtained far from compensation when the Gd coupling to the thermal bath is substantially weaker than that of Co; for λCo = 0.02 and λCo = 0.001, reversal occurs down to 1.5 at. % total Gd for selected pulse parameters. Increasing the Gd content accelerates reversal, consistent with the interpretation of Gd as an angular-momentum reservoir, whereas dilute interfacial Gd produces slower and more stochastic dynamics. These results show that compensation is not a fundamental requirement for ultrafast AO-HIS and identify the effective Gd spin-bath coupling as a key control parameter. Quantitative comparison with experiment will require explicit optical absorption, stack-dependent heat flow, dipolar fields, and a stable-final-state switching criterion.

infographic.key_insight: Atomistic simulations predict transient all-optical reversal in GdCo with just 1.5 at.% Gd, far from compensation, when Gd couples much more weakly to the thermal bath than Co.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Engineering species-dependent spin–bath coupling could enable low-Gd magnetic layers for ultrafast optical switching.
method: Simulated laser-driven dynamics using atomistic spin models under uniform heating.
Compared a three-monolayer Co film with surface-confined Gd against a uniformly alloyed three-dimensional GdCo model.
Varied Gd concentration, species-dependent spin–bath coupling, and pulse parameters.
infographic.evidence_signal: For selected pulse parameters, simulations showed transient toggle-like reversal down to 1.5 at.% total Gd, with faster reversal at higher Gd content.
infographic.watch_item: Transient reversal does not establish stable final-state switching; experimental validation requires optical absorption, stack-dependent heat flow, and dipolar fields.
infographic.paper_title: Atomistic Insights into the All-Optical Switching of GdCo Alloys with Minimal Gd Concentration
